kinds.label: the father-name
kinds.who: the father devises it; he announces it to the kindred of both sides
kinds.note: It stands first, and it remains unaltered, because it did not lie in the child's choice. In the early days a son's father-name was often a modification of the father's own (Finwë, Curufinwë) or a patronymic (Finwion, son of Finwë); a daughter's was as often drawn from her mother's.
kinds.gap: THE CORPUS GIVES NO QUENYA WORD FOR THIS KIND OF NAME. It names the rite and not the name. The form the received account supplies has no citable witness here.
kinds.cite: MR, Laws and Customs among the Eldar, Of Naming

kinds.label: the chosen name
kinds.who: the bearer, for themselves — a right every Noldorin child had, in which they may have differed from the other Eldar
kinds.when: at no fixed date, but not before the child could feel lámatyávë — individual pleasure in the sounds and forms of words; usually at or about the end of the tenth year
kinds.public: private, and private is not secret
kinds.note: A chosen name was personal property, like a ring or a cup: lendable, shareable with kin, and not to be taken without leave. To use it unpermitted was presumptuous or insulting. One might devise a new one later — the Eldar were deathless within Arda and by no means changeless — and the old name was not thereby abrogated: it stayed part of the full title.
kinds.gap: The Shibboleth gives the word and Laws and Customs does not: there Tolkien names only the CEREMONY, Essecilmë, and calls the name the chosen name in English. `kilmessi` is his own gloss — names of personal choice — and it occurs ONCE in the whole corpus. The variant `cilmessë` is carried by nine volumes and every one is tier 3.
kinds.cite: MR, Laws and Customs among the Eldar, Of Naming

kinds.label: the mother-name of insight
kinds.who: the mother, of her own choosing
kinds.when: in the hour of birth, or on some other occasion of moment
kinds.public: public if set immediately after the father-name; otherwise not
kinds.note: Also essi apacenyë, names of foresight. The mother named some dominant feature of the child's nature as she perceived it, or some foresight of its fate. These had authority and were true names when solemnly given, and in use they sometimes replaced the father-name and the chosen name both, within the family and without — though the father-name remained ever the true or primary name and a necessary part of any full title. They were given more often in the early days.
kinds.cite: MR, Laws and Customs among the Eldar, Of Naming

kinds.label: every other given name
kinds.who: anyone at all — not necessarily kin or house
kinds.when: in memory of a deed or an event, or for a marked feature of body or mind
kinds.note: These were NOT true names, and might not be recognised by the person they were applied to, unless actually adopted or self-given. They were seldom included in the full title; when they were, for wide use and fame, they came last and hedged — by some called Telcontar; sometimes known as Mormacil.
kinds.cite: MR, Laws and Customs among the Eldar, Of Naming

kinds.label: the after-name
kinds.who: others, in honour or in mockery
kinds.when: in the course of a life
kinds.note: The Shibboleth defines it in Tolkien's own words: an epessë is not necessarily given by the bearer's own kin, and is mostly given as a title of admiration or honour. It is the same class the Laws and Customs calls a given name that is not a true name; the archive keeps both words because the two texts use them, and does not merge them.
kinds.gap: LAWS AND CUSTOMS DOES NOT USE THIS WORD. It comes from the Shibboleth, and the relation between the two accounts is Tolkien's, not the archive's, to reconcile.

kinds.label: the full title
kinds.note: The sequence of all the names acquired in the course of life. The father-name first and always; the chosen name; a mother-name of insight where one was solemnly given; and at the end, hedged, any by-name famous enough to be worth recording.
kinds.cite: MR, Laws and Customs among the Eldar, Of Naming

people.name: Fëanor
people.note: The one life whose whole naming Tolkien set out himself.

names.name: Curufinwë
names.gloss: skilful Finwë — his father's name modified

names.name: Fëanáro
names.gloss: spirit of fire — Míriel's name for him

names.name: Fëanor
names.gloss: the Sindarised form the histories use
names.why: A form of the mother-name in another tongue is not a KIND of name. The corpus states the relation and does not state a class for the result.

names.name: Finwion
names.gloss: son of Finwë — the patronymic shape
names.why: Named in the Shibboleth among his names; the class is the archive's reading of the patronymic pattern Laws and Customs describes, not a statement in the text.

people.name: Galadriel
people.note: Her names are stated across two texts that do not agree in every particular, which is itself worth showing rather than smoothing.

names.name: Alatáriel
names.gloss: the Telerin name Celeborn gave her

names.name: Galadriel
names.gloss: the Sindarin form of Alatáriel, and the name history keeps
names.why: Again a translation of a name, not a kind. The archive will not invent a class for the form a name takes in another tongue.

people.name: Túrin
people.note: A man, not an Elf — and the whole point of including him. The Eldarin classes are not his; what he has is a life of by-names, most of them self-given, which is the one Eldarin category that fits Men without being imposed on them.

names.name: Neithan
names.gloss: the wronged — taken by himself among the outlaws
names.why: Self-given, so it is a true name by the Laws and Customs test. But that test is stated OF THE ELDAR, and Túrin is not one. The archive leaves the class blank rather than extend a rule past the people it was written about.

names.name: Gorthol
names.why: As above — a by-name of a Man.

names.name: Mormegil
names.why: As above. Note that Laws and Customs itself cites Mormacil, a variant of this name, as its own example of a by-name hedged into a full title.

note: The Eldarin system of several kinds of name, from Tolkien's own text. A kind carries a Quenya term ONLY where the corpus carries one: two of the four terms the received account gives have no citable witness here, and the silence is shown rather than filled. A name is classified only where a source states its kind.
